article.title: Midterm polls have good news, great news, and bad news for Democrats. Wait, what?
article.subtitle: The slightly complicated history of the generic ballot.

extraction.summary: Silver and McKown-Dawson introduce the Silver Bulletin 2026 generic congressional ballot polling average and use retroactively computed averages from midterms since 1994 to put the current D+5.3 reading in context. Three patterns stand out. The opposition party usually wins the House popular vote (by 4.4 points on average) and tends to gain about 2.5 points between late January and Election Day. Read by party label rather than in-party/out-party, though, the January generic ballot has historically overstated Democrats by 4.6 points. The authors attribute that bias to several factors and argue most of them do not apply in 2026; they restate their view, to be embedded in the FLIPR model, that the direction of polling bias is unpredictable. They also give the state benchmark formula (generic ballot + partisan lean × elasticity), the weights behind the partisan lean score, CES-based elasticity scores, and details on how likely-voter and registered-voter polls are treated, with the full midterms model to add a further LV adjustment.
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2026 generic congressional ballot polling average

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin generic ballot average includes two types of polls. The first asks which party's candidate the respondent will vote for in the U.S. House election, sometimes with named district candidates. The second asks which party the respondent prefers to control Congress.
findings.rationale: Empirically the two question types produce nearly identical results, and including both increases sample size.
findings.evidence_quote: We include these too since, empirically, they produce nearly identical results to the other type of survey and increase our sample size.

findings.statement: The generic ballot average weights each poll by quality, recency, sample size and partisan lean (house effect).

When a pollster publishes both likely-voter and registered-voter versions, the generic ballot average uses the likely-voter version. It slightly discounts the weight of registered-voter and all-adult polls but makes no further adjustment to their numbers.
findings.evidence_quote: We do prioritize likely voter polls over registered voter polls when pollsters list both, and slightly discount the weight associated with registered voter polls or polls of all adults.

findings.statement: The full FLIPR 2026 midterms model will apply an additional likely-voter adjustment to registered-voter and all-adult polls, which the 'simple' generic ballot average does not do.
findings.rationale: Midterm turnout is lower, and many registered voters reached by pollsters won't vote.
findings.evidence_quote: Our midterms model will make a further adjustment along these lines, but our “simple” generic ballot average does not.

findings.statement: In January 2026 only about 30% of the weight in the generic ballot average came from likely-voter polls. The authors give an illustration: a 2-point Democratic RV-to-LV 'enthusiasm gap' would put Democrats' likely-voter generic ballot edge at about 7 points, versus the D+5.3 average. The 2-point figure is a hypothetical, not an estimated parameter.

quantities.name: share of average weight from LV polls
hypothetical enthusiasm gap
quantities.context: illustrative difference between RV and LV polls favoring Democrats

quantities.name: implied LV edge
quantities.context: Democratic generic ballot lead among likely voters

findings.model_version: Silver Bulletin 2026 generic ballot average / FLIPR 2026
findings.evidence_quote: Currently, only about 30 percent of the weight in our generic ballot average comes from likely voter polls.

findings.statement: Republicans historically gained when pollsters switched from registered-voter to likely-voter screens. That pattern has now reversed: Democrats do well with highly engaged, college-educated voters and often benefit from lower turnout, so the generic ballot tends to get bluer as more pollsters adopt LV screens.
findings.evidence_quote: Until recently, Republicans tended to gain once pollsters switched over from registered voters to likely voters. But that tendency has now reversed.

findings.statement: Historical generic ballot averages for midterms from 1994 to 2022 were produced by retroactively applying the current Silver Bulletin polling average methodology to past generic ballot polls, at equivalent points in each cycle (285 days before Election Day).
findings.evidence_quote: the generic ballot as it appeared on equivalent days in midterm cycles since 1994 — that is, 285 days before Election Day — based on running our algorithm retroactively on past election cycles.

findings.statement: The correlation between the late-January generic ballot average and the eventual House popular vote in midterms since 1994 is 0.53.

quantities.name: correlation
quantities.context: January generic ballot vs House popular vote, midterms 1994-2022

findings.evidence_quote: The correlation between the generic ballot at this point in the cycle (early January) and the eventual House popular vote is 0.53

findings.statement: The empirical 95% margin of error of the January generic ballot average against the House popular vote margin is 5.7 points. Applied to D+5.3, that gives a range from D+11.0 to R+0.4.
findings.evidence_quote: the empirical margin of error on the January polling average, compared to the popular vote, is 5.7 points.

findings.statement: The margin of error of the generic ballot average against the House popular vote shrinks from 5.7 points in late January to 3.8 points on Election Day.

quantities.name: Election Day margin of error
quantities.context: generic ballot vs House popular vote

findings.evidence_quote: the generic ballot is fairly accurate on election day, with the margin of error shrinking to just 3.8 points.

findings.statement: The opposition party gains 2.5 points on the generic ballot on average between late January and Election Day in midterms since 1994. Applied to 2026, that would put Democrats at around +7.8.

quantities.name: average out-party gain
quantities.context: late Jan to Election Day, midterms 1994-2022

findings.evidence_quote: On average, the opposition party gains 2.5 points on the generic ballot between late January and Election Day.

findings.statement: Measured from the president's party's perspective, the opposition party won the House popular vote by 4.4 points on average in midterms since 1994. The in-party's average generic ballot margin was −3.6 on Election Day. Opposition gains between late January and Election Day by cycle, read from the chart: 1994 +4.1, 1998 +3.7, 2002 +1.7, 2006 +2.8, 2010 +5.8, 2014 +4.3, 2018 −1.2, 2022 −1.0.

quantities.name: average opposition House popular vote margin
in-party Election Day generic ballot average

findings.evidence_quote: the opposition party won the House popular vote by 4.4 points on average.

findings.statement: By party label, the late-January generic ballot has overestimated Democrats' eventual House popular vote margin by 4.6 points on average in midterms since 1994. The averages by stage are D+3.2 in late January, D+1.6 on Election Day, and D−1.4 in the actual House vote.

quantities.name: average overestimate of Democrats
quantities.context: Jan generic ballot vs House vote, 1994-2022

findings.evidence_quote: in midterms since 1994, the generic ballot at this stage of the race has overestimated Democrats’ eventual finish in the House popular vote by 4.6 points.

findings.statement: The FLIPR 2026 model will embed the longstanding Silver assumption that the direction of systematic polling bias is unpredictable from year to year, so the model does not adjust for an expected bias direction.
findings.rationale: Polls are often systematically biased (against Republicans in 2016, against Democrats in 2025), but predicting the direction in advance is usually futile.
findings.evidence_quote: we’d stand by our longstanding proposition, which will be embedded in our election model, that polling bias tends to be unpredictable from year to year.

findings.statement: The authors attribute the historical pro-Democratic bias of the January generic ballot to four factors. First, polls have tended to overrate Democrats recently. Second, Democrats were the in-party in 5 of the 8 midterms. Third, early polls use registered voters or adults, while midterm turnout is low. Fourth, the generic ballot and House vote diverge because of uncontested seats and top-two primaries such as California's.
findings.evidence_quote: What accounts for this historical bias? This answer isn’t quite so straightforward; it’s likely a combination of several factors.

findings.statement: Recent Democratic underperformance relative to polls has been concentrated in presidential years with Trump on the ballot. Polling was basically unbiased in 2018 and 2022, and Democrats considerably overperformed their polls in the 2025 off-year elections.
findings.evidence_quote: Polling was basically unbiased in 2018 and 2022, and Democrats considerably overperformed their polls in the off-year elections of 2025.

findings.statement: Differences between the generic ballot and the House popular vote caused by uncontested seats are mostly an accounting issue. Failing to nominate candidates lets the other party run up the popular vote but matters little for seats, as long as candidates run in competitive districts.
findings.evidence_quote: this is a technical accounting issue rather than a substantive one.

findings.statement: Silver Bulletin computes state-level benchmarks for 2026 as: Benchmark = generic ballot + partisan lean score × elasticity.
findings.model_version: Silver Bulletin 2026 generic ballot page / FLIPR 2026
findings.evidence_quote: Benchmark = generic ballot + partisan lean score * elasticity

findings.statement: The partisan lean score measures how a state voted relative to the nation. It weights the 2024 presidential election at 50%, the 2020 presidential election at 25%, and a rolling average of the past five state legislative elections at 25%.

quantities.name: state legislative weight
quantities.context: rolling average of past five elections

findings.evidence_quote: the formula gives 50 percent of the weight to the 2024 presidential election, 25 percent to the 2020 presidential election, and 25 percent to a rolling average of the past five state legislative elections.

findings.statement: The state legislative component of partisan lean uses the aggregate lower-chamber popular vote. Because many seats are uncontested, a regression-based method estimates what the aggregate vote would be if all seats were contested.
findings.rationale: Uncontested seats distort the raw aggregate vote.
findings.evidence_quote: we use some complicated math based on regression analysis to account for this. In essence, we estimate what the aggregate popular vote would be for the lower house if all seats were contested.

findings.statement: Elasticity measures how responsive a state is to national swings. It is high in states with many independents and swing voters, such as New Hampshire, and low in polarized states such as Mississippi. The 2026 scores were calculated from microdata in the 2022 and 2024 Cooperative Election Studies, each with about 60,000 respondents.
findings.evidence_quote: Our current elasticity scores, calculated from microdata in the 2022 and 2024 Cooperative Election Studies, which each surveyed 60,000 voters

findings.statement: State benchmarks at the D+5.3 generic ballot: NC D+2.6, ME D+12.7, GA D+1.9, MI D+5.4, AK R+8.4, and IA/TX/OH/FL between R+5 and R+6. At D+10 nationally, IA would be D+0.3, OH R+0.5 and AK R+2.3. Alaska's high elasticity makes it move fastest with the national environment.
findings.evidence_quote: Alaska gets a boost because of its high elasticity

findings.statement: A Senate benchmark deficit of 5 to 8 points can be overcome with strong candidates or weak opponents, but large candidate overperformances relative to partisanship are becoming rarer.
findings.evidence_quote: A benchmark in the range of −5 to −8 is just narrow enough that it can be overcome with strong candidates — or weak opponents — but large overperformances are getting rarer.

findings.statement: Before releasing their model, the authors judge Polymarket's 78% chance of a Democratic House takeover a good buy. They consider its 35% chance for the Senate roughly right but want race-by-race model precision before committing.
findings.rationale: The model sometimes introduces nuances that surprise them.
findings.evidence_quote: sometimes the model surprises us with the extra nuances it introduces!

findings.statement: As of January 2026, mid-decade redistricting is described as roughly a wash and the House map has little overall partisan bias, unlike the Senate map. A popular-vote win of about 4.4 points would therefore likely give Democrats the House. Ongoing redistricting fights are one reason the forecast had not yet launched.
findings.evidence_quote: redistricting has been something of a wash so far, and that the House map (as opposed to the Senate map) doesn’t currently have much overall bias.

findings.statement: The generic ballot average chart displays shaded bands within which 90% of polls are projected to fall. The average is updated nearly every day through November.

political_insights.insight: The president's party usually loses ground in midterms. Exceptions such as 1998 (Lewinsky overreach) and 2002 (Sept. 11) are attributed to unusual events.
political_insights.evidence: The opposition party won the House popular vote by 4.4 points on average since 1994.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Use a prior favoring the out-party in midterms.

political_insights.insight: The out-party's generic ballot advantage tends to grow over the course of the midterm year.
political_insights.evidence: Average gain of 2.5 points from late January to Election Day; it shrank only in 2018 and 2022.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Project drift toward the out-party in early-cycle forecasts.

political_insights.insight: Democrats now benefit from low turnout because of their strength among highly engaged, college-educated voters.
political_insights.evidence: The historical RV-to-LV shift toward Republicans has reversed.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: LV adjustments should now favor Democrats rather than Republicans.

political_insights.insight: Democrats' strong 2025 results were broadly consistent with an environment of about D+8.
political_insights.evidence: A small sample of races; Democrats overperformed their polls.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Special and off-year elections can serve as a check on the national environment.

political_insights.insight: Democrats recruited top Senate candidates for 2026 (Peltola in AK, Brown in OH, Cooper in NC). The authors contrast this with Republican candidate-quality problems in 2022.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Candidate quality could close benchmark gaps of 5-8 points.

political_insights.insight: Trump's approval is near its second-term low of net −14, and second terms sometimes see the bottom fall out.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Approval may push the environment further toward the out-party.

political_insights.insight: In wave elections, heavily gerrymandered seats can flip, turning gerrymanders into 'dummymanders', even though gerrymandering curbs the out-party's seat gains.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Seat translation should be nonlinear for large swings.

political_insights.insight: Republicans won the House popular vote by 2.7 points in 2022 and 2.6 points in 2024.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Even a narrow R popular-vote win could cost Republicans their slim majority.

references.description: Silver Bulletin 2026 generic congressional ballot polling average page, with state benchmark map
Cooperative Election Studies 2022 and 2024 (source for elasticity)

open_questions: How the FLIPR model adjusts registered-voter and all-adult polls to likely voters, and the size of that adjustment.
The exact weight discount applied to RV and all-adult polls in the generic ballot average.
How elasticity is computed from CES microdata.
The regression method used to impute contested lower-chamber state legislative votes.
Whether FLIPR applies the historical 2.5-point out-party drift as a prior.
How partisan lean is normalized relative to the nation, and whether its units are margin points.
Specific weights given to poll quality, recency and sample size in the average.
